title: 5.1.19 Lab: Delete the else, watch drift
description: Start from a working WASD movement pattern, delete the two else lines and watch the sprite drift, then restore them and set a speed of your own.

steps.title: Run as-is and confirm movement stops
steps.instructions: Click Run, then click the preview so it gets your keys. Hold a WASD key: the sprite moves. Release it: the sprite stops. That stop is the else-to-zero rule from 5.1.17 at work: each chain ends in an `else` line that sets the velocity back to 0.
hints: Velocity is explained in 5.1.15. In the moSHion docs drawer on the right, it is under Physics, on the page called Gravity and velocity.

steps.title: Delete the two else lines
steps.instructions: Find the two lines that say `else player.vel.x = 0;` and `else player.vel.y = 0;`. Delete both lines, then click Run.
hints: Look in draw() for the lines starting with `else` that set vel to 0.

steps.title: Tap a key once and watch the sprite drift
steps.instructions: Click the preview to focus it. Tap one WASD key briefly and release. Watch what happens: the sprite keeps moving because vel was never reset.
hints: The sprite drifts because velocity is not automatically reset between frames.

steps.title: Restore the else lines, then pick your speed
steps.instructions: Put both else lines back where they were, each at the end of its own chain (`else player.vel.x = 0;` and `else player.vel.y = 0;`), so the sprite stops when no key is held. Then make the speed your own: change the 4s and the -4s to another speed from 2 to 6, as 5.1.16's Try this did. Run it once more: the sprite moves at your speed and still stops the moment you let go. The grader checks that both else lines are back in draw() and that at least one movement line uses a speed other than 4.
hints: 5.1.16 shows the whole pattern again: if, else if, then the else that sets the speed back to 0.
Keep the minus sign on the `a` and `w` lines: `player.vel.x = -3;` moves left and `player.vel.x = 3;` moves right.

requirements.title: Restore else player.vel.x = 0
requirements.description: In draw() (or a function draw() calls), player.vel.x goes back to 0 when no left or right key is held, so the sprite stops sideways, and both keys still move it. The else line you put back, at the end of the same if / else if chain, does this. Setting it to 0 at the top of draw(), before the key checks, also counts, and so does one line with ? : that ends in 0. Help: 5.1.17 (The else-to-zero rule) and 5.1.16 (Movement pattern (if / else if / else))
requirements.hint: Put the else back at the end of the same if / else if chain it came from. An else under a separate if sets vel.x to 0 every frame the other key is up, so one key stops working.

requirements.title: Restore else player.vel.y = 0
requirements.description: In draw() (or a function draw() calls), player.vel.y goes back to 0 when no up or down key is held, so the sprite stops up and down, and both keys still move it. The else line you put back, at the end of the same if / else if chain, does this. Setting it to 0 at the top of draw(), before the key checks, also counts, and so does one line with ? : that ends in 0. Help: 5.1.17 (The else-to-zero rule) and 5.1.16 (Movement pattern (if / else if / else))
requirements.hint: Put the else back at the end of the same if / else if chain it came from. An else under a separate if sets vel.y to 0 every frame the other key is up, so one key stops working.

requirements.title: A speed of your own
requirements.description: At least one movement line in draw() (or a function draw() calls) sets player.vel.x or player.vel.y to a speed other than the starter's 4, so the sprite moves at a speed you chose (5.1.16 suggests 2 to 6). Help: 5.1.16 (Movement pattern (if / else if / else))

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote a moSHion sketch (p5-style JavaScript with a physics world) for the lab "5.1.19 Lab: Delete the else, watch drift". The task they were given: The starter ships a working WASD movement pattern in draw(): for each direction, an if / else if chain sets player.vel.x (or player.vel.y) from the keys and ends in an else that sets it back to 0. The student deletes both else lines, watches the sprite drift, then puts both else lines back so the sprite stops when no key is held, and changes the speed of 4 (and -4) to a speed of their own, from 2 to 6. What the starter file already had: exactly that working pattern, with a speed of 4 on every movement line. Because the starter already has both else lines, the first two criteria read as met on the starter; the speed criterion is the one the starter does not meet. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do when the sketch runs. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable and function names, if / else chains or ternaries, helper functions, template strings, arrow functions, semicolons, spacing, quotes and order are all fine. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment or inside a string never runs, so a line the student only wrote in a comment does not count. moSHion facts that matter here: kb.pressing('a') is true on every frame the key is held. vel.x and vel.y are the sprite's speed in pixels per frame, and a sprite keeps its velocity until code changes it, which is why it drifts when nothing sets the speed back to 0. An else belongs only to the if right above it. With two separate ifs, such as if (left) vel.x = -4; if (right) vel.x = 4; else vel.x = 0;, the else sets vel.x to 0 on every frame the right key is up, so the left key can never move the sprite. A chain written as if / else if / else, or 0 set at the top of draw() before separate ifs, does not have that problem. A function the student wrote counts only where it is called: a function that draw() (or update(), or another of their functions that draw() calls) calls by name runs every frame, a function only setup() calls runs once, and a function nothing calls never runs, so code that sits only inside it does not count. y grows downward, so a negative vel.y moves up. Write each note for THIS student's own code: in a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise. Write for a 14-year-old reader: short sentences and plain, everyday words.

rubric.title: Restore else player.vel.x = 0
rubric.description: In draw() (or a function the student wrote that draw() calls), when neither the left nor the right key is held, player.vel.x is set back to 0, so the sprite stops sideways. The else at the end of the chain is the shape the lab uses (with or without braces); any other way that sets vel.x to 0 whenever no left or right key is held also counts, such as setting it to 0 at the top of draw() before the key checks, or a ternary that ends in 0. If the else is put back under a separate if, so one of the two keys can never move the sprite, it is not met: say which key is undone. Help: 5.1.17 (The else-to-zero rule)

rubric.title: Restore else player.vel.y = 0
rubric.description: In draw() (or a function the student wrote that draw() calls), when neither the up nor the down key is held, player.vel.y is set back to 0, so the sprite stops up and down. The else at the end of the chain is the shape the lab uses (with or without braces); any other way that sets vel.y to 0 whenever no up or down key is held also counts, such as setting it to 0 at the top of draw() before the key checks, or a ternary that ends in 0. If the else is put back under a separate if, so one of the two keys can never move the sprite, it is not met: say which key is undone. Help: 5.1.17 (The else-to-zero rule)

rubric.title: A speed of your own
rubric.description: At least one movement line in draw() sets player.vel.x or player.vel.y to a speed other than 4 (or -4), so the sprite moves at a speed the student chose. 5.1.16 suggests 2 to 6, but any other speed that moves the sprite counts, including a decimal or a variable holding the speed. The lines that set the speed back to 0 are not a speed. If every movement line still uses 4, it is not met yet. Help: 5.1.16 (Movement pattern (if / else if / else))
